topic.title: Equivalent Representations of Polynomial and Rational Expressions
topic.summary: Factored and standard forms, polynomial long division, and the binomial theorem, and which form answers which question.

lesson.title: Equivalent Representations of Polynomial and Rational Expressions
lesson.summary: Factored and standard forms, polynomial long division, and the binomial theorem, and which form answers which question.
learningGoals: 1.11.A Rewrite polynomial and rational expressions in equivalent forms.
1.11.B Determine the quotient of two polynomial functions using long division.
1.11.C Rewrite the repeated product of binomials using the binomial theorem.
lesson.bigIdea: Equivalent analytic representations of the same function reveal different information. Factored form shows real zeros, holes, asymptotes, domain, and range. Standard form shows end behavior. Long division gives slant asymptotes, and the binomial theorem expands powers of binomials.
lesson.context: Earlier topics factored to find zeros, holes, and vertical asymptotes, and compared leading terms to find end behavior. This topic names those forms and adds two tools the CED requires: polynomial long division and the binomial theorem.

sections.title: 1.11.A · Factored form and standard form reveal different information.

blocks.text: Because the factored form of a polynomial or rational function readily provides information about real zeros, it can reveal x-intercepts, asymptotes, holes, domain, and range. The standard form of a polynomial or rational function can reveal its end behavior. The information from different analytic representations of the same function can be used to answer questions in context.

blocks.caption: What each form shows
rows: Degree, leading term, end behavior, y-intercept
Rational function with numerator and denominator in standard form

blocks.title: Watch the domain
blocks.text: Removing a common factor changes the domain. (x² − 4)/(x − 2) equals x + 2 only for x ≠ 2.

sections.takeaway: Decide what you need to find, then rewrite in the form that shows it.

sections.title: 1.11.B · Polynomial long division gives f(x) = g(x)q(x) + r(x).

blocks.text: Polynomial long division is an algebraic process similar to numerical long division involving a quotient and remainder. If the polynomial f is divided by the polynomial g, then f can be rewritten as f(x) = g(x)q(x) + r(x), where q is the quotient, r is the remainder, and the degree of r is less than the degree of g. Dividing by g(x) gives f(x)/g(x) = q(x) + r(x)/g(x).

To divide x² + 3x + 5 by x − 1: x · (x − 1) = x² − x, leaving 4x + 5; then 4 · (x − 1) = 4x − 4, leaving a remainder of 9. So x² + 3x + 5 = (x − 1)(x + 4) + 9, and (x² + 3x + 5)/(x − 1) = x + 4 + 9/(x − 1).

The result of polynomial long division is helpful in finding equations of slant asymptotes. As x increases or decreases without bound, 9/(x − 1) gets arbitrarily close to 0, so the slant asymptote is y = x + 4.

blocks.title: Write it like the AP Exam
blocks.text: Show the identity that checks the division: (x − 1)(x + 4) + 9 = x² + 3x + 5.

blocks.caption: Graph of (x² + 3x + 5)/(x − 1) with its slant asymptote y = x + 4
blocks.alt: A two-branch curve with a dashed vertical asymptote at x = 1; both branches approach the dashed slanted line y = x + 4.

sections.takeaway: The quotient gives the slant asymptote, and the remainder term approaches 0 at the ends.

sections.title: 1.11.C · The binomial theorem uses a row of Pascal's triangle to expand (a + b)ⁿ.

blocks.text: The binomial theorem uses the entries in a single row of Pascal's triangle to expand expressions of the form (a + b)ⁿ, including polynomial functions of the form p(x) = (x + c)ⁿ, where c is a constant. Row n gives the coefficients, the powers of a decrease from n to 0, and the powers of b increase from 0 to n.
For (x + 2)⁴, row 4 is 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, and the powers of 2 are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. So (x + 2)⁴ = x⁴ + 8x³ + 24x² + 32x + 16. For (2x − 1)³, use a = 2x and b = −1: 8x³ − 12x² + 6x − 1.

sections.takeaway: Use row n for the coefficients, and raise the whole of a and b, signs included, to their powers.

vocabulary.definition: Because the factored form of a polynomial or rational function readily provides information about real zeros, it can reveal information about x-intercepts, asymptotes, holes, domain, and range.
The standard form of a polynomial or rational function can reveal information about end behaviors of the function.

Polynomial long division is an algebraic process similar to numerical long division involving a quotient and remainder. If the polynomial f is divided by the polynomial g, then f can be rewritten as f(x) = g(x)q(x) + r(x), where q is the quotient, r is the remainder, and the degree of r is less than the degree of g.

The binomial theorem utilizes the entries in a single row of Pascal’s Triangle to more easily expand expressions of the form (a + b)ⁿ, including polynomial functions of the form p(x) = (x + c)ⁿ, where c is a constant.

connections.title: The quotient of leading terms, made exact
connections.body: Topic 1.7 found that the slant asymptote of (x² + 3x + 5)/(x − 1) is parallel to y = x. Long division gives the exact line, y = x + 4.
connections.transferQuestion: Which part of the divided form gives the slant asymptote?
connections.feedback: The quotient. The remainder term approaches 0 at the ends.

connections.title: Forms that show transformations
connections.body: Topic 1.12 writes functions as transformations of a parent function, such as a·f(x + h) + k. That form shows translations and dilations directly.
connections.transferQuestion: Compared with the graph of x², which way is the graph of (x − 3)² translated?

glossary.definition: The degree and sign of the leading term of a polynomial determines the end behavior of the polynomial function, because as the input values increase or decrease without bound, the values of the leading term dominate the values of all lower-degree terms.

A rational function is analytically represented as a quotient of two polynomial functions and gives a measure of the relative size of the polynomial function in the numerator compared to the polynomial function in the denominator for each value in the rational function’s domain.

When the graph of a rational function r has a horizontal asymptote at y = b, where b is a constant, the output values of the rational function get arbitrarily close to b and stay arbitrarily close to b as input values increase or decrease without bound. The corresponding mathematical notation is lim x→∞ r(x) = b or lim x→−∞ r(x) = b.

If the polynomial in the numerator dominates the polynomial in the denominator for input values of large magnitude, then the quotient of the leading terms is a nonconstant polynomial, and the original rational function has the end behavior of that polynomial. If that polynomial is linear, then the graph of the rational function has a slant asymptote parallel to the graph of the line.

If the value a is a real zero of the polynomial function in the denominator of a rational function and is not also a real zero of the polynomial function in the numerator, then the graph of the rational function has a vertical asymptote at x = a. Furthermore, a vertical asymptote also occurs at x = a if the multiplicity of a as a real zero in the denominator is greater than its multiplicity as a real zero in the numerator.

If the multiplicity of a real zero in the numerator is greater than or equal to its multiplicity in the denominator, then the graph of the rational function has a hole at the corresponding input value.
Because the factored form of a polynomial or rational function readily provides information about real zeros, it can reveal information about x-intercepts, asymptotes, holes, domain, and range.
The standard form of a polynomial or rational function can reveal information about end behaviors of the function.

Polynomial long division is an algebraic process similar to numerical long division involving a quotient and remainder. If the polynomial f is divided by the polynomial g, then f can be rewritten as f(x) = g(x)q(x) + r(x), where q is the quotient, r is the remainder, and the degree of r is less than the degree of g.

The binomial theorem utilizes the entries in a single row of Pascal’s Triangle to more easily expand expressions of the form (a + b)ⁿ, including polynomial functions of the form p(x) = (x + c)ⁿ, where c is a constant.
